cards.title: Processes vs threads
cards.text: Each process gets its own virtual address space. Threads inside one process share that memory, which makes them cheap to create but means they must coordinate access to shared data.

cards.title: Virtual memory
cards.text: Virtual memory gives every process the illusion of a large private memory. The OS maps virtual pages to physical RAM and can move rarely used pages out to disk.

cards.title: Recipe for deadlock
cards.text: A deadlock needs four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one and deadlock can't happen.

cards.title: Just a hobby
cards.text: In August 1991 Linus Torvalds announced Linux as “just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu”. It now runs most of the world's servers and every Android phone.

cards.question: What is it called when the OS saves one process's CPU state and loads another's?
A page fault happens when a program…
cards.answer: touches memory that isn't currently mapped in RAM

cards.question: Which CPU scheduling policy can starve long-running jobs?
cards.explanation: If short jobs keep arriving, a long job may never get the CPU.

cards.question: Which signal does `kill -9` send on Unix?
cards.explanation: SIGKILL can't be caught or ignored; SIGTERM (the default) politely asks the process to exit.

cards.question: What does a mutex guarantee?
cards.answer: Only one thread at a time in a critical section

cards.question: Which file on Unix-like systems lists the user accounts?
cards.explanation: Despite its name, password hashes moved to /etc/shadow long ago.

cards.question: What traditionally runs as process ID 1 on Unix-like systems?

cards.statement: A thread and a process are the same thing.
cards.explanation: A process is a running program with its own address space; threads are units of execution inside a process that share it.

cards.statement: A zombie process is one that is stuck burning CPU.
cards.explanation: A zombie has already exited; it lingers only as a process-table entry until its parent reads its exit status.

cards.statement: On Linux, devices such as disks and terminals appear as files under /dev.
cards.explanation: “Everything is a file” is a core Unix idea: you read and write many devices with ordinary file operations.

cards.statement: Adding more RAM always makes a computer faster.
cards.explanation: Extra RAM only helps if you were running short and swapping to disk; beyond that it sits unused.
L1 cache sits on the CPU core and answers in around a nanosecond; RAM takes roughly 100× longer.
A hard disk must physically move its head and wait for the platter: around 10 ms per random read.
